strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: adapting pretrained flow-matching models to parameter-dependent physical constraints without requiring paired state-parameter data during pretraining.
Combining weak-form PDE objectives, adjoint-matching fine-tuning, and an augmented latent-parameter flow is conceptually interesting and reasonably well motivated.

The Darcy experiments show meaningful reductions in residuals relative to a model trained on noisy data, while the proposed parameter regularization largely preserves pointwise mean, variance, and diversity statistics.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes useful architectural, optimization, computational-cost, and weak-test-function details.
weaknesses: The acoustic weak form appears mathematically inconsistent with the stated PDE. For spatially varying c, integrating -c^2 Δp against a test function produces ∇p·∇(c^2ψ), including a coefficient-gradient/interface term, whereas the paper retains only c^2∇p·∇ψ. The reported acoustic residual therefore corresponds more closely to a divergence-form operator than to the stated wave equation, undermining one of only two benchmark systems.

The central inverse-problem claim is insufficiently evaluated. Although ground-truth coefficient fields exist for both synthetic datasets, the paper reports no parameter-recovery error, posterior calibration, uncertainty metric, or comparison against inverse-problem baselines. Guidance results are almost entirely qualitative.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. There is no quantitative comparison against physics-informed generative training, physics-guided sampling, supervised joint state-parameter models, or standard inverse solvers. ECI is compared only visually on one boundary experiment, with hyperparameters selected by visual quality and acknowledged methodological differences.

Several experiments do not validate their advertised task directly: acoustic super-resolution has no high-resolution ground truth or field-error metric; boundary misspecification is assessed mainly through images; and sparse conditional generation lacks quantitative observation-fit and sample-quality results.

The theoretical guarantee from Adjoint Matching applies under restrictive conditions that the implementation violates or modifies: a nonzero running regularizer is used, the memoryless noise schedule is altered, deterministic inference follows stochastic training, and separate λx and λα scalings of gradients of a coupled terminal cost need not correspond to the gradient of any scalar objective. These choices may be practical, but the resulting method is more heuristic than the theoretical framing suggests.

Evidence for distribution preservation is limited to pointwise first- and second-moment statistics on one experiment. These metrics cannot rule out changes in spatial correlations, multimodal structure, or other forms of mode collapse. Results also lack multiple-run variability, and the acoustic table uses only 20 samples.

Even after fine-tuning, the Darcy strong residual is 5.6, substantially worse than the clean base model (0.83) and clean data (1.4). Thus weak-residual improvement does not establish recovery of genuinely high-quality physical samples.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear or inconsistent, including the exact terminal objective and weighting, the value of λα, and the surrogate parameter-flow definition in the algorithm versus the surrounding prose. Code and data-generation scripts are only promised for future release.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: enforcing PDE constraints in pretrained generative models while inferring unobserved physical parameters without paired parameter labels.

The combination of flow matching, weak-form PDE residuals, and joint state-parameter evolution is conceptually interesting. Weak residuals are particularly appropriate for noisy observations and avoid unstable high-order derivatives.

The paper covers several relevant settings—denoising, sparse-observation guidance, boundary-condition changes, and acoustic super-resolution—and reports meaningful residual reductions in the quantitative experiments.

The manuscript provides useful implementation details, including architectures, weak test functions, training costs, and hyperparameters, and it explicitly examines the effect of its parameter-space regularizer.
weaknesses: The central inverse-problem claim is inadequately validated. Although ground-truth permeability and sound-speed fields are available, the paper reports no quantitative parameter-recovery errors, posterior calibration, uncertainty metrics, or comparisons against supervised and physics-based inverse methods. Most evidence for latent-parameter recovery is visual.

The empirical comparisons are far too weak for a top-tier paper. There are no quantitative comparisons with physics-constrained flow/diffusion methods, direct test-time residual optimization, PINN-style inversion, or simpler post-training alternatives. The only ECI comparison is qualitative, selected by visual inspection, and explicitly acknowledged as not entirely fair.

Several headline experiments are incomplete. Guidance is evaluated only visually; boundary misspecification has no quantitative results; and acoustic “super-resolution” is assessed through residuals rather than accuracy against high-resolution solutions. Consequently, residual minimization or smoothing could explain the gains without demonstrating improved physical fidelity.

Distribution preservation is supported only by pointwise mean, variance, and diversity statistics. These metrics cannot detect changes in spatial correlations, joint distributions, multimodality, or sample quality. This is especially concerning because the unregularized method exhibits substantial distribution shift and parameter mode collapse.

The theoretical justification does not cleanly cover the proposed regularizer. The running cost is written as a function of the state but contains the trainable fine-tuned vector field and therefore depends on the control/model parameters. Standard adjoint-matching equations and the stated stop-gradient regression objective generally require modification for a control-dependent running cost; this issue is neither derived nor discussed.

The novelty is limited by directly adopting adjoint matching and standard weak-form residuals, with the main additions being an inverse predictor, residual output heads, and an empirical regularizer. Stronger ablations are needed to show that joint stochastic evolution is necessary relative to simply predicting parameters at the endpoint and optimizing the same residual.

Reported improvements remain mixed: in Darcy denoising, the fine-tuned strong residual is 5.6, substantially worse than 1.4 for clean data and 0.83 for the clean-data base model. The paper emphasizes relative improvement over a noisy model without establishing recovery to the desired clean distribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Code is only promised for future release, and important settings such as the observational noise magnitude, principal λx and λα values, guidance strength, data splits, and some numerical details are missing or scattered. Evaluation also uses small sample counts in places, such as 20 acoustic samples, without significance testing.

There are presentation and consistency issues, including an apparent base/fine-tuned parameter mismatch in Algorithm 1 and numerous typographical errors. More importantly, the paper does not clearly separate established guarantees inherited from adjoint matching from heuristic components that lack those guarantees.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: adapting pretrained generative models to satisfy parameter-dependent physical constraints without requiring paired state-parameter data during pretraining.

The combination of adjoint-matching fine-tuning, weak-form PDE rewards, and joint state-parameter evolution is conceptually interesting and appears meaningfully different from purely inference-time projection methods.
For Darcy flow, the use of compactly supported stochastic test functions is well motivated and reduces dependence on unstable high-order numerical derivatives.

The experiments cover several relevant settings—noisy observations, sparse conditioning, super-resolution, boundary enforcement, and misspecification—and the Darcy denoising results show substantial reductions in both weak and strong residuals while retaining pointwise diversity under regularization.
The appendix provides useful architectural, computational, and optimization details, including dataset generation, model sizes, training times, test-function construction, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The stated weak formulation for the heterogeneous acoustic equation appears mathematically incorrect. For spatially varying c, integrating -c^2 Delta p by parts produces an additional term involving grad(c^2), unless the PDE is instead written in divergence form. The paper omits this term despite using discontinuous binary c fields, directly weakening the validity of the acoustic residuals and conclusions.

The central claim of accurate latent-parameter recovery is not adequately evaluated. There is no paired parameter-reconstruction error, posterior calibration, coverage, or identifiability analysis. Pointwise distribution statistics do not establish that generated parameters correspond to their associated states, and the recovered binary fields visibly appear blurred or continuous.

There are essentially no competitive quantitative baselines. Tables compare only the base and fine-tuned models; ECI is included only as a qualitative, explicitly acknowledged unfair comparison. Comparisons with physics-constrained flow/diffusion training, projection methods, inverse solvers, or simpler reward-fine-tuning alternatives are needed.

The theoretical connection to Adjoint Matching is incomplete. The proposed regularizer f depends on the learned vector field/control, although it is treated as a state cost in the adjoint derivation. It is therefore unclear whether the stated lean-adjoint dynamics and consistency guarantees remain applicable. Likewise, the surrogate latent-parameter flow is heuristic and lacks justification that it recovers a meaningful joint distribution.

Evidence that the learned distribution is preserved is limited to pointwise means, variances, and marginal diversity. These measures cannot detect changes in spatial correlations, multimodality, or state-parameter coupling, so the associated claim is stronger than the evidence.

The evaluation is restricted to two synthetic PDE families, with several headline tasks supported mainly by visual examples. Sparse guidance has no quantitative observation error or comparison, misspecified-boundary performance lacks numerical metrics, and reported uncertainty is across generated samples rather than independent training runs.

Important reproducibility details remain missing, including the observational-noise magnitude, data splits, random-seed variability, and several guidance and loss weights. Code and data-generation scripts are only promised for future release.

Overall, the idea is promising, but the acoustic-formulation issue, lack of direct inverse-recovery validation, and absence of strong quantitative baselines are major shortcomings rather than minor omissions.

strengths: The paper presents a technically interesting framework that extends Adjoint Matching to joint state–parameter dynamics, enabling post-training enforcement of parameter-dependent physical constraints without paired state–parameter training data.
Weak-form PDE residuals are well motivated for noisy and discontinuous fields, and the appendix provides useful derivations for Darcy flow, elasticity, Helmholtz, and Stokes systems.

The experimental scope is broad: four distinct PDE families cover observation noise, boundary-condition shifts, and model misspecification, complemented by sparse-observation guidance and a natural-image demonstration.

The authors examine the trade-off between physical consistency and distributional fidelity using weak and strong residuals, MMD, diversity measurements, and parameter-preserving regularization. Full hyperparameter sweeps are reported in the appendix.

The method appears computationally practical after base-model training, particularly for Darcy, and the scaled memoryless-noise observation provides a modest theoretical and practical extension of Adjoint Matching.
weaknesses: The central claim of accurate latent-parameter recovery is not convincingly evaluated. Parameter MMD only compares marginal distributions and does not establish that the inferred parameter for a particular state is correct. The paper lacks paired reconstruction errors, correlations with ground-truth fields, posterior coverage, or identifiability analysis. Because the inverse predictor and generated state can adapt jointly to minimize the same residual, low residuals and marginal MMD can coexist with incorrect state–parameter pairings.

Baseline coverage and fairness are insufficient. PBFM is used in a deliberately misspecified post-training setting that the authors explicitly acknowledge disadvantages a training-time method, and it is modified using the proposed inverse predictor. ECI is tested only for elasticity. Comparisons to physics-guided inference methods, oracle supervised joint models, retraining on target simulations, and standard Bayesian inverse solvers are missing.

The theoretical guarantee is limited relative to the implemented method. Consistency with a reward-tilted distribution is inherited for an ideal memoryless process, whereas experiments use a step-size-regularized schedule, clipping, time-step subsampling, surrogate parameter dynamics, additional running costs, and deterministic final sampling. There is no analysis showing what joint distribution the full practical algorithm targets or whether its parameter component is statistically meaningful.

Evaluation uses only 256 generated samples and apparently a single training run per configuration. Reported deviations describe variation across samples rather than variability across independent training seeds, so optimization stability and statistical significance are unclear. Extensive hyperparameter sweeps combined with reporting representative best configurations further raise model-selection concerns.

Residual evaluation is closely aligned with the training physics, discretization, and synthetic reference generation. Independent solver validation, mesh-refinement tests, evaluation at unseen resolutions, and genuinely out-of-distribution parameter families are absent, leaving open the possibility of discretization-specific residual optimization.

Several quantitative results reveal substantial limitations: residuals often remain several times above those of clean target data; the Stokes state-distribution MMD can deteriorate severely; and improvements over simpler Adjoint Matching variants are inconsistent across systems. The presentation sometimes overstates these trade-offs as broad physical validity.

The natural-image experiment is largely qualitative, covers only two class–prompt examples, and reports no PickScore, diversity, or human-preference statistics. It therefore provides weak support for the claimed cross-domain utility.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the lengthy appendix: important weak-test-function settings such as the number of tests, scale ranges, jitter, and wavelet probability are not specified in the manuscript, and the claimed released configurations/code are not concretely available here.

strengths: The paper addresses an important setting: adapting pretrained flow-matching generators to changed physical constraints without requiring paired state-parameter data during pretraining.
Combining weak-form PDE residuals, Adjoint Matching, and a jointly evolved latent-parameter field is conceptually interesting and potentially useful for scientific generative modeling.
The experimental scope is broad, covering four distinct PDE systems, sparse-observation guidance, boundary and model misspecification, and a natural-image demonstration.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, full hyperparameter sweeps, non-curated samples, and useful ablations of the parameter flow and inverse predictor.
weaknesses: The central inverse-problem claim is insufficiently validated. Parameter recovery is evaluated primarily through marginal MMD, without sample-wise recovery error, posterior calibration, uncertainty coverage, or an identifiability analysis. A learned parameter distribution can have favorable MMD while assigning incorrect parameters to individual states.

The results do not substantiate the strong claim of producing physically valid solutions. Reported residuals are normalized by clean reference solutions, yet the best models commonly remain several times above the reference weak residual. On Darcy, the proposed joint model also has substantially worse strong residuals than PBFM, revealing a concerning gap between the optimized weak objective and actual pointwise PDE satisfaction.

Boundary-condition enforcement is incomplete. Compactly supported test functions eliminate boundary terms, and explicit boundary penalties or boundary-error measurements are not consistently presented outside elasticity. Thus, interior weak residuals alone do not demonstrate satisfaction of the full boundary-value problems.

Baseline coverage and fairness are inadequate. PBFM is evaluated in a deliberately misspecified setting for which the paper acknowledges that it is disadvantaged, and it uses a much smaller batch size. ECI is evaluated only for elasticity and with a substantially different sampling budget. Relevant inference-time constraint and inverse-problem baselines are not compared across the main benchmarks.

The evaluation appears to use one training run per configuration. Error bars seemingly measure variation across generated samples rather than variation across independent training runs, and no significance analysis is given. Moreover, representative configurations are selected separately by their best residual or MMD after large hyperparameter sweeps, without a validation-based selection protocol.

The theoretical justification applies to an idealized continuous-time memoryless schedule, whereas the implementation modifies the singular coefficient, discretizes trajectories, subsamples and clips losses, and finally samples deterministically. The paper does not establish that the claimed tilted-distribution consistency survives these changes, nor provide adequate ablations of the new noise-scaling parameter.

The natural-image experiment is limited to qualitative examples from two classes/prompts. It reports neither PickScore nor diversity, fidelity, or human-preference measurements, so it does not provide convincing evidence for the claimed cross-domain utility.

Several metrics have limited interpretability: high-dimensional raw-field MMD with a comparison-dependent median bandwidth does not directly establish distributional fidelity, and the residual normalizations and aggregation of physically different Stokes equations are not sufficiently justified. Overall, the work is substantial but the evidence is not reliable enough to support its principal claims at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: adapting pretrained flow-matching models to satisfy parameter-dependent physical constraints without requiring paired state–parameter data during pretraining.

The joint evolution of states and latent physical parameters is a meaningful extension of adjoint matching, supported by a clearly described residual architecture and a theoretical justification for the scaled memoryless noise schedule.
The use of randomized weak-form PDE residuals is well motivated for noisy observations and avoids unstable higher-order differentiation.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering Darcy flow, elasticity, Helmholtz propagation, Stokes flow, sparse-observation guidance, and a natural-image recoloring example.

The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, including model architectures, residual derivations, training algorithms, hyperparameters, dataset generation, computational costs, and extensive non-curated samples.
Ablations expose useful trade-offs among physical residual, distributional fidelity, and diversity; several experiments show clear improvements over the base flow model.
weaknesses: The central inverse-problem claim is not convincingly validated. Parameter recovery is evaluated primarily through marginal MMD, which does not establish that each generated parameter is correctly paired with its state. Ground-truth parameter error, correlation, joint-distribution metrics, posterior calibration, and uncertainty coverage are absent despite being available for the synthetic benchmarks.

The baseline suite is incomplete and partly unfavorable by construction. The paper explicitly notes that PBFM is disadvantaged by the imposed physics mismatch, while ECI is evaluated only for elasticity. Comparisons to direct latent-parameter optimization, inference-time PDE guidance, posterior-sampling methods, and paired-data or oracle inverse baselines would better contextualize the contribution.

Many reported outputs remain substantially less physical than the clean reference distribution: normalized strong residuals are around 46 for a representative Darcy configuration, 3.8 for elasticity, and 10.5 for Helmholtz. Thus, statements that samples are physically valid or that constraints are enforced are stronger than the evidence supports.

Results use only 256 evaluation samples and apparently single training runs; the displayed deviations seem to measure variation across samples rather than variation across independent training seeds. Reliability and sensitivity to initialization are therefore unclear, especially given extensive hyperparameter sweeps and favorable configuration selection.

The claimed preservation of the learned distribution is inconsistent across tasks. Some configurations exhibit large MMD shifts or reduced parameter diversity, and the paper provides no principled rule for choosing the three trade-off hyperparameters without access to target reference data.

Sparse-observation inference is demonstrated only qualitatively, without reconstruction error, comparison baselines, or posterior-quality measurements. The natural-image extension is likewise limited to qualitative results on two classes, with no PickScore, diversity, or content-preservation evaluation.

The scaled-noise lemma is technically plausible but relatively incremental, and several practical heuristics—time-grid tilting, clipping, step subsampling, and endpoint regularization—lack targeted ablations. This makes it difficult to separate the contribution of joint parameter evolution from the broader engineering package.

There are reproducibility ambiguities despite the extensive appendix: the text refers to released configuration files and future code release rather than providing a clearly accessible artifact, and Algorithm 1 uses ambiguous state notation when evaluating and advancing the base versus fine-tuned trajectories.
